planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in spring into consistently moist, acidic, sandy-peaty soil in full sun to light shade among wiregrass; avoid any fertilizer or rich organic amendment.

directions: Large spreading pogonia grows in the open, wet-to-mesic longleaf pine savannas and seepage-slope bogs of the Coastal Plain, from the mid-Atlantic south into the Florida panhandle and west along the Gulf into Louisiana, where periodic fire keeps the wiregrass understory open enough for light to reach it. A single grasslike leaf sheaths the lower stem, which rises to one or two large rose-pink, nodding flowers with a crested, fringed lip held well above the ground on wiry stalks in late spring. It is distinguished from the related rose pogonia by its taller stature, larger flowers, and preference for drier, less saturated savanna margins rather than true saturated sphagnum bog. Best grown in a dedicated bog bed with sharp sand or peat kept constantly damp but not standing in water, alongside pitcher plants and wiregrass.

planting.note: Set nursery-propagated divisions in spring into deep, well-drained but seasonally damp sandy soil in full sun; establishment is slow and plants may skip flowering in dry or disturbed years. Also catalogued in some current sources as Eulophia ecristata or Orthochilus ecristatus.

directions: Giant orchid occupies the drier, sandy margins of pine flatwoods and longleaf savannas across Florida, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and east Texas, often appearing in open ground the season after a fire clears competing vegetation. A rosette of tall, strap-shaped pleated leaves sends up a stout flower spike in mid-to-late summer bearing numerous small, maroon-brown and yellow-green blooms that lack the crest found on related genera, giving the species its common name. It depends on specific mycorrhizal fungi and is exceedingly slow from seed, so garden stock should come only from nursery-propagated divisions sold occasionally by Florida native plant specialists. Give it lean, sharply drained sand with only moderate, seasonal moisture rather than a saturated bog setting.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring into moist, acidic, nutrient-poor sandy soil in full sun; southern milkweed needs the open, seasonally saturated conditions of a wet pine savanna rather than a typical dry milkweed bed.

directions: Southern milkweed is a slender, little-known Coastal Plain species restricted to wet pine flatwoods and savannas of the Florida panhandle, Georgia, and Alabama, where it grows among wiregrass and pitcher plants in consistently damp, acidic sand. Its narrow, pale green leaves and clusters of small, pale greenish-white flowers are far more understated than the familiar orange and pink milkweeds, and it is most often noticed by the latex-filled stems and slim seed pods rather than showy bloom. Like other milkweeds it serves as a monarch and queen butterfly host plant, but its narrow habitat requirements make it a specialist choice for a sunny, wet, sandy bog garden rather than a general pollinator bed. Avoid rich or fertilized soil, which it does not tolerate.

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface of moist, acidic, sandy soil in fall so winter moisture and cold help break dormancy; keep the site open and free of heavy leaf litter.

directions: Low pine-barren milkwort occupies the seasonally saturated flats and seepage edges of longleaf pine savannas and pitcher-plant bogs from the Carolinas to Florida and west along the Gulf into Louisiana, where fire keeps the ground open. Its branching, candelabra-like stems carry small, clustered yellow flower heads through summer and fall, smaller and more numerous than the solitary dense spikes of orange milkwort. It behaves as a short-lived annual or biennial, reseeding reliably where soil stays consistently damp, acidic, and free of competing thatch. Pair it with pitcher plants, sundews, and meadow beauties in a sunny, wet, sandy bog garden rather than ordinary garden beds.

planting.note: Scatter seed on moist, open, acidic sandy or peaty soil in fall; germination follows winter chilling and spring moisture in a wet pine savanna or bog-garden setting.

directions: Drumheads is a true annual of wet pine savannas, pitcher-plant bog margins, and seasonally flooded ditches along the Coastal Plain, easily told from other milkworts by its leaves arranged in tight whorls of four that form a distinctive cross along the stem. Dense, cube-shaped heads of small rosy-magenta to purple flowers top wiry stems from late summer into fall, giving the plant its drumhead-like common name. It depends on open, saturated, acidic sand free of heavy competition and reseeds dependably where that disturbance-maintained wetness persists year to year. Grow it in a sunny bog garden or the damp fringe of a rain garden rather than typical mixed borders.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (Weakley)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun to light shade; it colonizes readily by rhizome in ditches and savanna seeps and spreads faster than most other meadow beauties.

directions: West Indian meadow beauty grows in the wettest, most consistently saturated pockets of pine savannas, roadside ditches, and flatwoods seeps across Florida, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, extending south into the Caribbean. Its stems and calyx are noticeably glandular-hairy compared with other Rhexia, and its smaller, rose-pink four-petaled flowers with curved yellow anthers open in succession through summer above narrower, more pointed leaves. It spreads more aggressively by rhizome than Maryland or savanna meadow beauty, forming loose colonies in standing shallow water or saturated sand. Site it at the wettest edge of a bog garden or rain garden where few other perennials tolerate near-constant moisture.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into moist-to-wet, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; plants form a grasslike basal rosette the first year before flowering in subsequent seasons.

directions: Bristleleaf chaffhead grows in the wetter, seasonally saturated longleaf pine savannas of the Florida panhandle, Alabama, Georgia, and Mississippi, where its narrow, grasslike, bristle-tipped basal leaves blend in with surrounding wiregrass until bloom time. In late summer and fall it sends up slender flowering stems topped with flat clusters of lavender-purple button flowers that, unlike vanilla plant, carry no coumarin fragrance, making the bristly basal leaves the more reliable way to tell the two apart. It is fire-adapted and flowers most heavily the growing season following a dormant-season burn, resprouting readily from its woody rootstock. Give it full sun and consistently damp, acidic, sandy soil rather than the drier sandhill conditions preferred by most of its chaffhead relatives.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated corms in spring into wet-to-mesic, acidic, sandy soil in full sun; flowering is strongly tied to recent fire history, so expect sparse bloom without periodic disturbance mimicking burns.

directions: Many-flowered grass pink is the smallest-statured and most fire-dependent of the Calopogon species, occurring in wet-to-mesic longleaf pine savannas from North Carolina to Florida and west into Alabama and Mississippi. A single grasslike leaf accompanies a short stem bearing as many as fifteen small magenta-pink flowers that open just a few at a time, a denser raceme than tuberous grass pink's more open spike. Populations bloom most heavily in the one to two growing seasons immediately following a dormant-season fire, then decline as woody competition returns, so established plantings benefit from mimicking that disturbance with periodic cutting back. Grow corms from specialty native orchid sources in full sun and consistently wet, acidic, nutrient-poor sand alongside pitcher plants and wiregrass.
